paragraphs: The checklists on this page are prompts for self-reflection only, not hiring criteria, personality evaluations or conclusions about ability. Authorization and boundaries vary considerably for RFID specialists: authority over site surveys, tag selection, tag data writing and system launch approval belongs to different roles. No checklist replaces checking the actual authority and project scope of the target position.

First observe whether you can break vague tracking requirements into objects, processes, tags and environmental conditions, and determine whether existing systems can be reused. Then complete a full exercise using fictional materials F1—F5 in the entry module: check tag selection, read rates and data fields, and flag items requiring confirmation or escalation. The exercise requires only paper and text files, with no real tags, readers or customer systems needed.

Signals worth considering include willingness to repeatedly test read rates under site conditions, accurately record failures and boundaries, and accept that business and project leads decide launches. Reasons for caution include treating one experiment's read rate as a universal conclusion or changing site configurations and production data without authorization.

This card's conclusions come from public occupational task information and editorial synthesis. They are not your personal assessment results and do not predict employment outcomes. RFID specialists' actual tasks depend on the employer, industry and project boundaries; the same Chinese title may involve entirely different duties and authority at different companies.

If you are willing to connect physical sites with information systems and use experiments and data to assess feasibility, this work is worth exploring. First clarify three matters when assessing a position: whether you can independently conduct site surveys and recommend tag selection, who approves system configuration and production data changes, and to whom you escalate inadequate read rates.

The same person often connects several aspects of RFID specialist work, but they differ in nature: some involve surveys and selection based on site conditions, some use read-rate data to assess solutions, and others use interface and data rules to determine integration feasibility. Considering these separately helps identify the abilities a position actually requires.

entries: Requirements analysis | Translate business tracking needs into technical requirements | Identify operational requirements, gather information on existing hardware, software, networks and key business processes, and translate needs into technical requirements for tags, readers and software.

Solution design | Design tag and reader combinations | Select tag types and mounting locations according to object materials, environment and processes, determine reader placement and integration methods, and compare candidate solutions using models or simulations.

Site survey | Analyze site conditions and obstacles | Survey sites to determine system configurations, affected processes and implementation obstacles, and adjust designs and implementation plans accordingly.

Testing and validation | Test read rates and system functions | Test tag reading and writing and software functions, conduct acceptance testing on newly installed or updated systems, and check that applications follow architectural standards and established practices.

Integration and deployment | Connect to business systems and launch | Integrate tags, readers and software into existing systems, define data fields and interfaces, and coordinate launches and cutovers with business teams.

Support and documentation | Train users and maintain documentation | Provide technical training and support to users, write process documents, work instructions and operating procedures, and record equipment and process details.

values: Materials and Scenario | All Data Are Fictional and Editorially Designed

You are a project engineer at the fictional Yuansu Supply Chain Technology company. Review selection and test records for distribution center project P-3110 and recommend launch, corrective action or review. All materials and values below are entirely fictional, not real customers, equipment or test results.

F1 Requirements and process: the distribution center handles about 8,000 shipping boxes daily and needs automatic records at receiving, sorting and shipping; the existing WMS accepts interface data. F2 Objects and environment: three categories—cardboard boxes, plastic totes and metal pallets; the sorting area has metal shelving and forklift aisles; ambient temperature is 5—35 ℃. F3 Tags and equipment: candidate ultra-high-frequency tags A (cardboard boxes), B (plastic totes) and C (metal pallets); 4 fixed readers and 2 handheld readers. F4 Test data: read rates of 99.2% for cardboard boxes, 98.7% for plastic totes and 82.4% for metal pallets (project requirement ≥ 95%); near metal shelving, the rate drops to 76%. F5 Conclusion and approval section: the draft says Overall requirements met; ready for launch, but retest and business confirmation fields are blank.
Task

Check F1—F5 item by item and state which results meet requirements, which need correction, which information is insufficient, and which unconfirmed items and approver must be included in the launch recommendation.
Do not add equipment models, read rates or authorization information absent from the scenario; list unknowns separately.
Reference Deliverables

Meets requirements: cardboard boxes at 99.2% and plastic totes at 98.7% both meet the project requirement (≥ 95%). Requires correction: metal pallets at 82.4% fall below the requirement, and the rate drops to 76% near metal shelving; adjust tag types or mounting locations and add readers if necessary before retesting. Requires verification: whether tag C is optimized for metal, the extent of metal-related interference with reading, and business confirmation of data fields and processes.

The launch recommendation must state that metal pallets fail requirements and retest and business confirmation fields are blank, and must be approved by an authorized role. The engineer only submits recommendations.

This exercise involves no real customers, real equipment or real production data. Actual selection, testing and launch follow employer and customer procedures. If you cannot judge, you may write Insufficient basis to judge and explain what evidence is missing.
